        ("resolvable rungs in the cap", f"{cap_capacity(1.0, EPS, MARGIN)}"),
        ("threshold-statistic separation", "1  (Lipschitz constant: none finite)"),
    ]
    for name, value in rows:
        print(f"  {name:<34} {value}")
    print()
    print("  Bottom line: for any stable statistic the resolving power of this experiment")
    print("  is capped at 0.0141 regardless of how many times it is repeated; the only")
    print("  decisive tests available are discontinuous ones.")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__.split("Run with:")[0].rstrip())
    demo_1_chordal_geometry()
    demo_2_power_ceiling()
    demo_3_replication()
    demo_4_sharpness()
    demo_5_alignment_window()
    demo_6_optimal_smooth_test()
    demo_7_capacity()
    demo_8_holder()
    demo_9_discontinuous_escape()
    demo_10_summary()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: End-to-End Spherical-Cap Diagnostics for a Near-Threshold Correlation Test
demos.description: A complete, dependency-free numerical tour of the theory on an explicit configuration realising the recorded readings 0.558 and 0.550 against a common response. In ten sections it verifies the chordal identity to machine precision; computes the chordal and angular radii of the cap and checks the Jordan-inequality bound; tabulates the power ceiling and the sensitivity required for a decisive verdict; demonstrates exact replication invariance up to dimension 200000; confirms that the distance statistic attains the ceiling and that correlation is 1-Lipschitz on the sphere by exhaustive search over unit-vector pairs; derives the alignment window forced by the recorded margin; constructs the contrast direction and shows by a full sweep of test directions that it is optimal; tabulates cap capacity and the Hölder ceilings; and finally exhibits the discontinuous threshold statistic separating the same configuration completely while violating every candidate Lipschitz constant.
demos.code:
"""
Spherical-Cap Power Ceiling for Near-Threshold Correlation Tests
================================================================

Numerical demonstration of the geometry of near-threshold hypothesis testing.

Setting.  A predictor u in R^n is compared with a response w through the
scale-invariant summary

    corr(u, w) = <u, w> / (||u|| ||w||),

so the experiment sees u only through its direction  u_hat = u / ||u||, a point
on the unit sphere.  Two competing hypotheses -- "the dial reads 0.558" and
"the dial sits exactly on the pre-registered floor 0.550" -- are realised by two
directions u_hat, v_hat.

The results demonstrated here:

  1. Chordal identity          ||u_hat - v_hat||^2 = 2 - 2 corr(u, v)
  2. Cap bound                 corr >= 1 - eps  ==>  chord <= sqrt(2 eps)
  3. Angular form              arccos(c) <= (pi/2) sqrt(2 - 2c)
  4. Power ceiling             |F(u_hat) - F(v_hat)| <= L sqrt(2 eps)
                               for every L-Lipschitz-on-the-sphere F --
                               NO dependence on the sample size n
  5. Replication invariance    corr(rep_m u, rep_m v) = corr(u, v) exactly
  6. Sharpness                 F(x) = L ||x - v_hat||  attains the ceiling
  7. Alignment window          a margin delta caps alignment at 1 - delta^2/2
  8. Optimal smooth test       correlation against the contrast direction
                               (u_hat - v_hat)/||u_hat - v_hat|| separates the
                               hypotheses by exactly the chordal distance,
                               which is the maximum over the smooth class
  9. Cap capacity              at most floor(L sqrt(2 eps) / delta) resolvable
                               rungs fit inside the cap; here exactly one
 10. The discontinuous escape  a threshold statistic separates the same
                               configuration by 1 and is Lipschitz for no L

Run with:  python3 demo.py
Requires only the standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = Sequence[float]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Euclidean primitives
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dot(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    """Standard inner product <u, v> = sum_i u_i v_i."""
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))


def norm(u: Vector) -> float:
    """Euclidean norm ||u|| = sqrt(<u, u>)."""
    return math.sqrt(dot(u, u))


def normalise(u: Vector) -> List[float]:
    """The direction u_hat = u / ||u|| (the zero vector is returned unchanged)."""
    n = norm(u)
    if n == 0.0:
        return list(u)
    return [x / n for x in u]


def corr(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    """Scale-invariant correlation <u, v> / (||u|| ||v||)."""
    return dot(u, v) / (norm(u) * norm(v))


def chord(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    """Chordal distance ||u_hat - v_hat|| between the two directions."""
    uh, vh = normalise(u), normalise(v)
    return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(uh, vh)))


def replicate(u: Vector, m: int) -> List[float]:
    """rep_m(u): the concatenation of m copies of u, modelling m replications."""
    return [x for _ in range(m) for x in u]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The reference configuration (R)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

READING_CROSSED: float = 0.558      # pooled reading of the "crossed" hypothesis
READING_FLOOR: float = 0.550        # pre-registered floor, "not crossed"
MARGIN: float = round(READING_CROSSED - READING_FLOOR, 12)   # delta = 0.008
EPS: float = 1.0e-4                 # alignment slack: corr(u, v) >= 1 - eps


def reference_configuration() -> Tuple[List[float], List[float], List[float]]:
    """Construct u, v, w in R^2 realising the two recorded readings.

    Both predictors are placed on the same side of the response w = (1, 0) at the
    angles forced by their readings, which makes them maximally aligned with each
    other:  corr(u, w) = 0.558, corr(v, w) = 0.550, corr(u, v) >= 0.9999.
    """
    w: List[float] = [1.0, 0.0]
    angle_u: float = math.acos(READING_CROSSED)
    angle_v: float = math.acos(READING_FLOOR)
    u: List[float] = [math.cos(angle_u), math.sin(angle_u)]
    v: List[float] = [math.cos(angle_v), math.sin(angle_v)]
    return u, v, w


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def correlation_statistic(w: Vector) -> Callable[[Vector], float]:
    """x |-> corr(x, w).  Exactly 1-Lipschitz on the unit sphere (Cauchy-Schwarz)."""
    return lambda x: corr(x, w)


def distance_statistic(reference: Vector, L: float) -> Callable[[Vector], float]:
    """x |-> L ||x - reference||.  Globally L-Lipschitz; attains the ceiling."""
    ref = list(reference)
    return lambda x: L * math.sqrt(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(x, ref)))


def contrast_direction(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> List[float]:
    """e = (u_hat - v_hat) / ||u_hat - v_hat||, the optimal smooth test direction."""
    uh, vh = normalise(u), normalise(v)
    d = [a - b for a, b in zip(uh, vh)]
    nd = norm(d)
    if nd == 0.0:
        raise ValueError("the two hypotheses coincide: no smooth test separates them")
    return [x / nd for x in d]


def threshold_statistic(w: Vector, t: float) -> Callable[[Vector], float]:
    """The discontinuous rank/threshold rule: 1 if corr(x, w) >= t, else 0."""
    return lambda x: 1.0 if corr(x, w) >= t else 0.0


def separation(F: Callable[[Vector], float], u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    """|F(u_hat) - F(v_hat)|: what the statistic can see between the hypotheses."""
    return abs(F(normalise(u)) - F(normalise(v)))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Diagnostics derived from the theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cap_radius(eps: float) -> float:
    """Chordal radius sqrt(2 eps) of a cap of alignment 1 - eps."""
    return math.sqrt(2.0 * eps)


def power_ceiling(L: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """The sample-size-free ceiling L sqrt(2 eps)."""
    return L * cap_radius(eps)


def lipschitz_needed(delta: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Sensitivity required for a separation delta inside an eps-cap."""
    return delta / cap_radius(eps)


def alignment_ceiling(delta: float) -> float:
    """A recorded margin delta caps the mutual alignment at 1 - delta^2 / 2."""
    return 1.0 - delta * delta / 2.0


def cap_capacity(L: float, eps: float, delta: float) -> int:
    """Largest number of monotone rungs an L-Lipschitz statistic resolves in the cap."""
    return int(math.floor(power_ceiling(L, eps) / delta))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def demo_1_chordal_geometry() -> None:
    banner("1.  Chordal geometry of the correlation cap")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    c = corr(u, v)
    print(f"  corr(u, w)               = {corr(u, w):.6f}   (crossed reading)")
    print(f"  corr(v, w)               = {corr(v, w):.6f}   (floor)")
    print(f"  recorded margin delta    = {MARGIN:.6f}")
    print(f"  mutual alignment corr(u,v) = {c:.9f}")
    print()
    print("  Chordal identity  ||u_hat - v_hat||^2 = 2 - 2 corr(u, v):")
    print(f"    left  side  = {chord(u, v) ** 2:.12e}")
    print(f"    right side  = {2 - 2 * c:.12e}")
    print(f"    discrepancy = {abs(chord(u, v) ** 2 - (2 - 2 * c)):.3e}")
    print()
    theta = math.acos(c)
    print(f"  chordal distance         = {chord(u, v):.8f}")
    print(f"  angular distance         = {theta:.8f} rad = {math.degrees(theta):.5f} deg")
    print(f"  Jordan bound (pi/2)*chord= {math.pi / 2 * chord(u, v):.8f} rad  (>= angle: "
          f"{math.pi / 2 * chord(u, v) >= theta})")
    print()
    print(f"  Cap of alignment 1 - {EPS:g}:")
    print(f"    chordal radius sqrt(2 eps) = {cap_radius(EPS):.8f}  ( = sqrt(2)/100 )")
    ang = math.acos(1 - EPS)
    print(f"    angular radius arccos(1-eps) = {ang:.8f} rad = {math.degrees(ang):.5f} deg")
    print(f"    below 0.9 degrees?          {math.degrees(ang) < 0.9}")
    print(f"    is the configuration inside the cap?  chord <= radius: "
          f"{chord(u, v) <= cap_radius(EPS)}")


def demo_2_power_ceiling() -> None:
    banner("2.  The sample-size-free power ceiling")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    print("  Ceiling  |F(u_hat) - F(v_hat)| <= L sqrt(2 eps)  for eps = 1e-4:")
    for L in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 10.0, 70.71):
        print(f"    L = {L:6.2f}   ceiling = {power_ceiling(L, EPS):.6f}")
    print()
    print("  Sensitivity required for a given separation:")
    for delta in (MARGIN, 0.05, 0.5, 1.0):
        print(f"    delta = {delta:5.3f}   L >= {lipschitz_needed(delta, EPS):9.4f}")
    print()
    print("  A full verdict (separation 1) demands L >= 70.71: a statistic that moves")
    print("  seventy units per unit of movement on the sphere.")
    print()
    print("  Actual separations achieved on the configuration:")
    F_corr = correlation_statistic(normalise(w))
    print(f"    response correlation      : {separation(F_corr, u, v):.8f}")
    e = contrast_direction(u, v)
    F_contrast = correlation_statistic(e)
    print(f"    contrast correlation      : {separation(F_contrast, u, v):.8f}")
    F_dist = distance_statistic(normalise(v), 1.0)
    print(f"    distance statistic (L=1)  : {separation(F_dist, u, v):.8f}")
    print(f"    ceiling at L = 1          : {power_ceiling(1.0, EPS):.8f}")


def demo_3_replication() -> None:
    banner("3.  Replication does not help")
    u, v, _ = reference_configuration()
    base = corr(u, v)
    print("  m-fold replication multiplies <.,.> by m and each norm by sqrt(m);")
    print("  the factors cancel exactly, so correlation and chord are invariant.")
    print()
    print(f"  {'m':>8} {'dimension':>10} {'corr(rep u, rep v)':>22} {'chord':>14} "
          f"{'ceiling (L=1)':>15}")
    for m in (1, 2, 5, 50, 1000, 100000):
        ru, rv = replicate(u, m), replicate(v, m)
        print(f"  {m:>8} {2 * m:>10} {corr(ru, rv):>22.15f} {chord(ru, rv):>14.10f} "
              f"{power_ceiling(1.0, EPS):>15.10f}")
    print()
    print(f"  Maximum deviation from the unreplicated alignment {base:.15f}: "
          f"{max(abs(corr(replicate(u, m), replicate(v, m)) - base) for m in (2, 5, 50, 1000)):.3e}")
    print("  Increasing the sample size buys no resolution for a smooth statistic.")


def demo_4_sharpness() -> None:
    banner("4.  The ceiling is sharp, and the class is non-vacuous")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    print("  (a) The distance statistic F(x) = L ||x - v_hat|| is exactly L-Lipschitz")
    print("      and attains the ceiling L * chord(u, v):")
    for L in (0.5, 1.0, 3.0):
        F = distance_statistic(normalise(v), L)
        got, want = separation(F, u, v), L * chord(u, v)
        print(f"      L = {L:4.1f}   achieved = {got:.10f}   L*chord = {want:.10f}   "
              f"match = {abs(got - want) < 1e-12}")
    print()
    print("  (b) Correlation against a unit response is 1-Lipschitz on the sphere;")
    print("      a random sample of unit-vector pairs never violates the inequality:")
    F = correlation_statistic(normalise(w))
    worst = 0.0
    steps = 400
    for i in range(steps):
        for j in range(steps // 8):
            a, b = 2 * math.pi * i / steps, 2 * math.pi * j * 8 / steps
            x, y = [math.cos(a), math.sin(a)], [math.cos(b), math.sin(b)]
            d = math.hypot(x[0] - y[0], x[1] - y[1])
            if d > 0:
                worst = max(worst, abs(F(x) - F(y)) / d)
    print(f"      largest observed |F(x) - F(y)| / ||x - y|| = {worst:.10f}  (<= 1: {worst <= 1 + 1e-12})")


def demo_5_alignment_window() -> None:
    banner("5.  The alignment window forced by the recorded margin")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    print(f"  A reading gap delta forces chord >= delta, hence corr(u, v) <= 1 - delta^2/2.")
    print(f"    recorded margin delta        = {MARGIN:.6f}")
    print(f"    |corr(u,w) - corr(v,w)|      = {abs(corr(u, w) - corr(v, w)):.10f}")
    print(f"    chord(u, v)                  = {chord(u, v):.10f}   (>= delta: "
          f"{chord(u, v) >= MARGIN - 1e-12})")
    print(f"    alignment ceiling 1 - d^2/2  = {alignment_ceiling(MARGIN):.9f}")
    print(f"    attained alignment           = {corr(u, v):.9f}")
    print()
    print("  So every realisation of the two readings has")
    print(f"      0.999900 <= corr(u, v) <= {alignment_ceiling(MARGIN):.6f},")
    print(f"  a window of width {alignment_ceiling(MARGIN) - 0.9999:.3e}.")


def demo_6_optimal_smooth_test() -> None:
    banner("6.  The optimal smooth test: correlation against the contrast direction")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    e = contrast_direction(u, v)
    F_e = correlation_statistic(e)
    F_w = correlation_statistic(normalise(w))
    sep_e, sep_w = separation(F_e, u, v), separation(F_w, u, v)
    print(f"  contrast direction e = ({e[0]:+.6f}, {e[1]:+.6f}),  ||e|| = {norm(e):.12f}")
    print(f"  separation of the contrast test  = {sep_e:.10f}")
    print(f"  chordal distance                 = {chord(u, v):.10f}   (equal: "
          f"{abs(sep_e - chord(u, v)) < 1e-12})")
    print(f"  separation of the response test  = {sep_w:.10f}")
    print(f"  improvement factor               = {sep_e / sep_w:.6f}")
    print(f"  theoretical cap on improvement   = {cap_radius(EPS) / MARGIN:.6f}")
    print()
    print("  Optimality check: no 1-Lipschitz-on-the-sphere statistic can beat the chord.")
    print("  Sweeping every correlation direction on the circle:")
    best, best_angle = 0.0, 0.0
    for k in range(3600):
        a = 2 * math.pi * k / 3600
        s = separation(correlation_statistic([math.cos(a), math.sin(a)]), u, v)
        if s > best:
            best, best_angle = s, a
    contrast_angle = math.atan2(e[1], e[0]) % (2 * math.pi)
    print(f"    best separation over all directions = {best:.10f}")
    print(f"    chordal distance                    = {chord(u, v):.10f}")
    print(f"    maximising direction angle {best_angle:.5f} rad; contrast angle "
          f"{contrast_angle:.5f} rad")
    print("    (the two differ by pi: +e and -e give the same absolute separation)")


def demo_7_capacity() -> None:
    banner("7.  Cap capacity: how many rungs fit inside the cap")
    print("  A monotone ladder gaining delta per rung, with endpoints aligned at 1 - eps,")
    print("  satisfies  k * delta <= L sqrt(2 eps).")
    print()
    print(f"  {'L':>6} {'eps':>10} {'delta':>8} {'L sqrt(2 eps)':>15} {'k_max':>7}")
    for L, eps, delta in ((1.0, EPS, MARGIN), (1.0, EPS, 0.004), (1.0, EPS, 0.002),
                          (2.0, EPS, MARGIN), (1.0, 1e-3, MARGIN)):
        print(f"  {L:>6.1f} {eps:>10.0e} {delta:>8.4f} {power_ceiling(L, eps):>15.8f} "
              f"{cap_capacity(L, eps, delta):>7d}")
    print()
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    F = correlation_statistic(normalise(w))
    gain = F(normalise(u)) - F(normalise(v))
    print(f"  At the recorded instance the bound is k <= {cap_capacity(1.0, EPS, MARGIN)}, and one rung")
    print(f"  really is resolvable: the response correlation gains {gain:.6f} = the margin.")
    print("  Capacity of the cap: exactly one rung.")


def demo_8_holder() -> None:
    banner("8.  Holder statistics: softening continuity does not remove the ceiling")
    print("  |F(x) - F(y)| <= C ||x - y||^alpha  ==>  separation <= C (sqrt(2 eps))^alpha.")
    print()
    r = cap_radius(EPS)
    print(f"  {'alpha':>7} {'ceiling at C=1':>17} {'C needed for full separation':>32}")
    for alpha in (1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25):
        print(f"  {alpha:>7.2f} {r ** alpha:>17.8f} {1.0 / r ** alpha:>32.4f}")
    print()
    print("  Smaller exponents buy a milder constant only by making the statistic more")
    print("  singular at small scales: resolution is always paid for in local instability.")


def demo_9_discontinuous_escape() -> None:
    banner("9.  The escape: a discontinuous threshold statistic")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    t = 0.554
    F = threshold_statistic(normalise(w), t)
    print(f"  Threshold rule at t = {t} (the midpoint of the two readings):")
    print(f"    F(u_hat) = {F(normalise(u)):.1f}   [corr = {corr(u, w):.4f} >= t]")
    print(f"    F(v_hat) = {F(normalise(v)):.1f}   [corr = {corr(v, w):.4f} <  t]")
    print(f"    separation = {separation(F, u, v):.1f}  -- maximal, inside a 0.81-degree cap.")
    print()
    print("  No contradiction: the rule is Lipschitz for no constant.  For any candidate L")
    print("  we exhibit two unit vectors straddling the cut at distance < 1/L:")
    print()
    print(f"  {'candidate L':>13} {'||x - y||':>14} {'|F(x) - F(y)|':>15} {'L||x-y||':>12} "
          f"{'violated?':>11}")
    s = math.sqrt(1 - t * t)
    for L in (1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1.0e4, 1.0e8):
        d = min(t / 2, 1.0 / (2 * (abs(L) + 1)))
        x = [t, s]                      # unit vector, corr(x, w) = t exactly
        y = [t - d, s]                  # corr(y, w) < t: the rule drops to 0
        gap = abs(F(x) - F(y))
        dist = math.hypot(x[0] - y[0], x[1] - y[1])
        print(f"  {L:>13.1e} {dist:>14.3e} {gap:>15.1f} {L * dist:>12.4f} "
              f"{str(gap > L * dist):>11}")
    print()
    print("  The verdict of the threshold rule flips under a perturbation of the predictor")
    print("  far smaller than the cap itself: sharpness is bought with brittleness.")


def demo_10_summary() -> None:
    banner("10.  Summary table for the recorded near-threshold instance")
    u, v, w = reference_configuration()
    e = contrast_direction(u, v)
    rows: List[Tuple[str, str]] = [
        ("recorded readings", f"{READING_CROSSED} vs {READING_FLOOR} (margin {MARGIN})"),
        ("attained alignment corr(u,v)", f"{corr(u, v):.9f}"),
        ("alignment ceiling 1 - d^2/2", f"{alignment_ceiling(MARGIN):.9f}"),
        ("chordal cap radius sqrt(2 eps)", f"{cap_radius(EPS):.8f}"),
        ("angular cap radius", f"{math.degrees(math.acos(1 - EPS)):.5f} deg  (< 0.9 deg)"),
        ("chord of the configuration", f"{chord(u, v):.8f}"),
        ("ceiling for L = 1", f"{power_ceiling(1.0, EPS):.8f}"),
        ("response-correlation separation", f"{separation(correlation_statistic(normalise(w)), u, v):.8f}"),
        ("contrast-correlation separation", f"{separation(correlation_statistic(e), u, v):.8f}"),
        ("max improvement factor", f"{cap_radius(EPS) / MARGIN:.4f}"),
        ("L needed for a full verdict", f"{lipschitz_needed(1.0, EPS):.4f}"),
        ("resolvable rungs in the cap", f"{cap_capacity(1.0, EPS, MARGIN)}"),
        ("threshold-statistic separation", "1  (Lipschitz constant: none finite)"),
    ]
    for name, value in rows:
        print(f"  {name:<34} {value}")
    print()
    print("  Bottom line: for any stable statistic the resolving power of this experiment")
    print("  is capped at 0.0141 regardless of how many times it is repeated; the only")
    print("  decisive tests available are discontinuous ones.")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__.split("Run with:")[0].rstrip())
    demo_1_chordal_geometry()
    demo_2_power_ceiling()
    demo_3_replication()
    demo_4_sharpness()
    demo_5_alignment_window()
    demo_6_optimal_smooth_test()
    demo_7_capacity()
    demo_8_holder()
    demo_9_discontinuous_escape()
    demo_10_summary()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Replication-Invariance Stress Test and Exhaustive Smooth-Test Optimality Sweep
demos.description: Two focused numerical experiments targeting the least intuitive claims. Experiment A repeats the configuration up to one hundred thousand times, reaching dimension 200000, and shows that the correlation and the chordal distance are preserved to floating-point precision, so the ceiling is literally the same real number in every dimension. Experiment B sweeps 200000 test directions on the circle and confirms that no correlation statistic separates the hypotheses by more than the chordal distance, with the maximum attained exactly at the contrast direction; it then generates twenty thousand random 1-Lipschitz statistics of infimal-convolution form and verifies that none of them exceeds the same ceiling.
demos.code:
"""Replication-invariance stress test and smooth-test optimality sweep.

Two numerical experiments that make the two most counter-intuitive claims tangible.

Experiment A. Replication invariance.
  Repeating a coordinate vector m times multiplies every inner product by m and every
  norm by sqrt(m), so the correlation -- and hence the chordal distance and the power
  ceiling -- is left exactly unchanged. We verify this to machine precision for m up to
  a hundred thousand, i.e. in dimensions up to 200000, and confirm that the largest
  separation available to a 1-Lipschitz statistic is literally the same real number in
  every one of those dimensions.

Experiment B. Optimality of the contrast test.
  We exhaustively sweep the test direction over a fine grid of the sphere (a circle in
  dimension two, a spherical grid in dimension three) and confirm that the maximum
  separation over all correlation statistics equals the chordal distance, attained at the
  contrast direction (u_hat - v_hat)/||u_hat - v_hat|| -- and that a randomly generated
  family of 1-Lipschitz statistics never exceeds it.

Run:  python3 replication_and_optimality.py
Standard library only.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = Sequence[float]


def dot(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))


def norm(u: Vector) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(dot(u, u))


def normalise(u: Vector) -> List[float]:
    n = norm(u)
    return [x / n for x in u]


def corr(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return dot(u, v) / (norm(u) * norm(v))


def chord(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    uh, vh = normalise(u), normalise(v)
    return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(uh, vh)))


def replicate(u: Vector, m: int) -> List[float]:
    return [x for _ in range(m) for x in u]


def configuration_2d() -> Tuple[List[float], List[float], List[float]]:
    w = [1.0, 0.0]
    u = [math.cos(math.acos(0.558)), math.sin(math.acos(0.558))]
    v = [math.cos(math.acos(0.550)), math.sin(math.acos(0.550))]
    return u, v, w


def experiment_a() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("A.  Replication invariance of the correlation, the chord and the ceiling")
    print("=" * 74)
    u, v, _ = configuration_2d()
    base_corr, base_chord = corr(u, v), chord(u, v)
    print(f"  {'m':>8} {'dimension':>10} {'|corr - corr_1|':>18} {'|chord - chord_1|':>19}")
    for m in (1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000):
        ru, rv = replicate(u, m), replicate(v, m)
        print(f"  {m:>8} {2*m:>10} {abs(corr(ru, rv) - base_corr):>18.3e} "
              f"{abs(chord(ru, rv) - base_chord):>19.3e}")
    print()
    print(f"  The ceiling for a 1-Lipschitz statistic is sqrt(2e-4) = {math.sqrt(2e-4):.10f}")
    print("  in every one of these dimensions. Sample size is simply not a parameter of it.")
    print()


def experiment_b() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("B.  The contrast direction is the optimal smooth test")
    print("=" * 74)
    u, v, w = configuration_2d()
    uh, vh = normalise(u), normalise(v)
    d = [a - b for a, b in zip(uh, vh)]
    e = [x / norm(d) for x in d]
    target = chord(u, v)

    best, best_a = 0.0, 0.0
    grid = 200000
    for k in range(grid):
        a = 2 * math.pi * k / grid
        s = abs(dot(uh, [math.cos(a), math.sin(a)]) - dot(vh, [math.cos(a), math.sin(a)]))
        if s > best:
            best, best_a = s, a
    print(f"  exhaustive sweep over {grid} test directions:")
    print(f"    best separation found        = {best:.12f}")
    print(f"    chordal distance             = {target:.12f}")
    print(f"    contrast-test separation     = "
          f"{abs(dot(uh, e) - dot(vh, e)):.12f}")
    print(f"    sweep exceeds the chord?      {best > target + 1e-12}")
    print()

    print("  random 1-Lipschitz statistics of the form F(x) = min_j (c_j + ||x - p_j||):")
    rng = random.Random(20260902)
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(20000):
        pts = [[rng.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(2)] for _ in range(3)]
        pts = [normalise(p) for p in pts]
        offs = [rng.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in pts]

        def F(x: Vector, pts: List[List[float]] = pts,
              offs: List[float] = offs) -> float:
            return min(c + math.dist(list(x), p) for c, p in zip(offs, pts))

        worst = max(worst, abs(F(uh) - F(vh)))
    print(f"    largest separation over 20000 random such statistics = {worst:.12f}")
    print(f"    chordal ceiling                                      = {target:.12f}")
    print(f"    any violation?                                        {worst > target + 1e-12}")
    print()
    print("  Conclusion: the maximum of the separation over the smooth class is exactly the")
    print("  chordal distance, and an ordinary correlation attains it.")


def main() -> None:
    experiment_a()
    experiment_b()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Spherical-Cap Diagnostic for Near-Threshold Hypothesis Pairs
algorithms.description: Given two hypothesised predictors and a response, this procedure computes every quantity the geometry determines: the mutual alignment rho, the chordal cap radius sqrt(2 - 2 rho), the angular radius together with its certified Jordan bound (pi/2) times the chord, the reading gap delta, the power ceiling L times the chord for a statistic of sensitivity L, the sensitivity 1/chord that a fully decisive verdict would demand, the alignment ceiling 1 - delta^2/2 that the reading gap forces, the number of resolvable ladder rungs, and a consistency flag verifying that the claimed margin and the claimed alignment can coexist. The mathematical foundation is the chordal identity together with the ceiling |F(u-hat) - F(v-hat)| <= L ||u-hat - v-hat|| valid for every statistic Lipschitz on the unit sphere. Complexity is three inner products and three norms, i.e. O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; crucially the outputs do not depend on the sample size, so the diagnostic can be run at the design stage before any data exist. In the pipeline it is the entry point: it decides whether a proposed smooth test is capable in principle of the verdict the study wants.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  u, v : hypothesised predictor vectors in R^n (nonzero)
       w    : response vector in R^n (nonzero)
       L    : sensitivity (Lipschitz constant on the sphere) of the intended statistic
OUTPUT a diagnostic record

 1  rho   <- <u,v> / (||u|| ||v||)                 // mutual alignment
 2  rho   <- clamp(rho, -1, +1)                    // guard against rounding
 3  chord <- sqrt(max(0, 2 - 2*rho))               // chordal identity
 4  theta <- arccos(rho)                           // angular radius, radians
 5  assert theta <= (pi/2) * chord                 // Jordan's inequality
 6  delta <- | <u,w>/(||u|| ||w||) - <v,w>/(||v|| ||w||) |
 7  ceiling <- L * chord                           // power ceiling: sample-size-free
 8  if chord = 0 then needed <- +infinity else needed <- 1 / chord
 9  alignment_ceiling <- 1 - delta^2 / 2           // the margin caps the alignment
10  if delta = 0 then rungs <- 0 else rungs <- floor(ceiling / delta)
11  feasible <- (delta <= chord + tolerance)       // margin and alignment consistent?
12  RETURN (rho, chord, theta, delta, ceiling, needed, alignment_ceiling, rungs, feasible)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: the spherical-cap diagnostic for a near-threshold correlation test.

Given two hypothesised predictors and a response, the diagnostic reports the geometry
that governs every stable test statistic: the mutual alignment of the hypotheses, the
chordal and angular radius of the cap they occupy, the power ceiling at a given
sensitivity, the sensitivity a decisive verdict would require, and the alignment ceiling
that the observed reading gap forces. All quantities are O(n) in the data dimension and
none of them depends on the sample size.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Sequence

Vector = Sequence[float]


def dot(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))


def norm(u: Vector) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(dot(u, u))


def corr(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    """Scale-invariant correlation; requires u, v nonzero."""
    return dot(u, v) / (norm(u) * norm(v))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CapDiagnostic:
    """Everything the geometry determines about a near-threshold test."""
    alignment: float          # rho = corr(u, v)
    chord: float              # ||u_hat - v_hat|| = sqrt(2 - 2 rho)
    angular_radius_deg: float # arccos(rho) in degrees
    jordan_bound_deg: float   # (pi/2) * chord, the certified angular upper bound
    reading_gap: float        # delta = |corr(u,w) - corr(v,w)|
    ceiling: float            # L * chord, the largest separation a stable test can see
    sensitivity_needed: float # 1 / chord, for a fully decisive verdict
    alignment_ceiling: float  # 1 - delta^2 / 2, forced by the reading gap
    resolvable_rungs: int     # floor(ceiling / delta)
    feasible: bool            # is the reading gap compatible with the alignment?


def cap_diagnostic(u: Vector, v: Vector, w: Vector, sensitivity: float = 1.0) -> CapDiagnostic:
    """Run the full diagnostic.

    Complexity: three inner products and three norms, i.e. O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

    Mathematical content:
      * chordal identity      ||u_hat - v_hat||^2 = 2 - 2 corr(u, v);
      * power ceiling         |F(u_hat) - F(v_hat)| <= L ||u_hat - v_hat||  for every F
                              that is L-Lipschitz on the unit sphere -- with no dependence
                              on the dimension n, hence none on the sample size;
      * angular form          arccos(rho) <= (pi/2) sqrt(2 - 2 rho)  (Jordan's inequality);
      * alignment ceiling     a reading gap delta forces corr(u, v) <= 1 - delta^2 / 2;
      * cap capacity          a monotone ladder gaining delta per rung has at most
                              floor(L sqrt(2 eps) / delta) rungs inside the cap.
    """
    rho = max(-1.0, min(1.0, corr(u, v)))
    chord = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 2.0 - 2.0 * rho))
    delta = abs(corr(u, w) - corr(v, w))
    ceiling = sensitivity * chord
    return CapDiagnostic(
        alignment=rho,
        chord=chord,
        angular_radius_deg=math.degrees(math.acos(rho)),
        jordan_bound_deg=math.degrees(math.pi / 2 * chord),
        reading_gap=delta,
        ceiling=ceiling,
        sensitivity_needed=(float("inf") if chord == 0.0 else 1.0 / chord),
        alignment_ceiling=1.0 - delta * delta / 2.0,
        resolvable_rungs=(0 if delta == 0.0 else int(math.floor(ceiling / delta))),
        feasible=(delta <= chord + 1e-12),
    )


def report(d: CapDiagnostic, sensitivity: float = 1.0) -> str:
    """Human-readable rendering of the diagnostic."""
    lines = [
        f"alignment corr(u, v)          : {d.alignment:.9f}",
        f"chordal cap radius            : {d.chord:.8f}",
        f"angular radius                : {d.angular_radius_deg:.5f} deg "
        f"(certified <= {d.jordan_bound_deg:.5f} deg)",
        f"reading gap delta             : {d.reading_gap:.6f}",
        f"power ceiling at L = {sensitivity:<8.3g}: {d.ceiling:.8f}",
        f"sensitivity for a verdict     : L >= {d.sensitivity_needed:.4f}",
        f"alignment ceiling 1 - d^2/2   : {d.alignment_ceiling:.9f}",
        f"resolvable rungs in the cap   : {d.resolvable_rungs}",
        f"geometry consistent           : {d.feasible}",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # The recorded near-threshold instance: readings 0.558 and 0.550 against a common response.
    w = [1.0, 0.0]
    u = [math.cos(math.acos(0.558)), math.sin(math.acos(0.558))]
    v = [math.cos(math.acos(0.550)), math.sin(math.acos(0.550))]
    print(report(cap_diagnostic(u, v, w, sensitivity=1.0), 1.0))

algorithms.name: Construction of the Optimal Smooth Test via the Contrast Direction
algorithms.description: This procedure returns the single best statistic in the stable class, together with a certificate that it is best. Normalising the two hypotheses and forming the contrast direction e = (u-hat - v-hat)/||u-hat - v-hat||, the correlation statistic x -> corr(x, e) separates the hypotheses by exactly the chordal distance, because all three vectors are unit so correlations against e are inner products and <u-hat - v-hat, e> = ||u-hat - v-hat||. Since no statistic 1-Lipschitz on the sphere can exceed that distance, the value is simultaneously attained and maximal: the supremum over the smooth class is a maximum, realised by an ordinary correlation. The routine also reports the improvement factor over any baseline direction, typically the response, which quantifies exactly how much is left on the table by the test actually being run. Complexity is O(n) time and O(n) space, dominated by two normalisations.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  u, v : hypothesised predictor vectors in R^n (nonzero, distinct as directions)
OUTPUT e    : the optimal test direction; sep : its separation; a proof of optimality

1  u_hat <- u / ||u||;   v_hat <- v / ||v||
2  d     <- u_hat - v_hat
3  if ||d|| = 0 then ABORT: the hypotheses coincide as directions,
                     and NO smooth statistic separates them
4  e   <- d / ||d||                                 // the contrast direction, a unit vector
5  sep <- corr(u_hat, e) - corr(v_hat, e)           // equals <d, e> = ||d||
6  ceiling <- ||d||                                 // max over all 1-Lipschitz-on-sphere F
7  assert |sep - ceiling| <= tolerance              // the optimum is attained
8  // optional comparison with a baseline direction b (e.g. the response w):
9  base <- | <u_hat, b/||b||> - <v_hat, b/||b||> |
10 improvement <- ceiling / base
11 RETURN (e, sep, ceiling, improvement)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: construction of the optimal smooth test (correlation against the contrast
direction) with a certificate of optimality.

Among all statistics that are 1-Lipschitz on the unit sphere, the one that separates two
hypothesis directions by the largest possible amount is the correlation against the
contrast direction e = (u_hat - v_hat) / ||u_hat - v_hat||. Its separation equals the
chordal distance ||u_hat - v_hat|| exactly, and no member of the class exceeds that value,
so the optimum over the smooth class is attained by an ordinary correlation statistic.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence

Vector = Sequence[float]


def dot(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))


def norm(u: Vector) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(dot(u, u))


def normalise(u: Vector) -> List[float]:
    n = norm(u)
    if n == 0.0:
        raise ValueError("cannot normalise the zero vector")
    return [x / n for x in u]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OptimalSmoothTest:
    direction: List[float]        # the contrast direction e, a unit vector
    separation: float             # corr(u_hat, e) - corr(v_hat, e) = chordal distance
    ceiling: float                # the maximum over all 1-Lipschitz-on-the-sphere statistics
    is_optimal: bool              # separation == ceiling, up to floating-point error
    statistic: Callable[[Vector], float]   # x |-> corr(x, e)


def optimal_smooth_test(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> OptimalSmoothTest:
    """Build the optimal smooth test for the pair of hypotheses (u, v).

    Complexity: two normalisations and one difference, i.e. O(n) time, O(n) space.

    Correctness. Write u_hat, v_hat for the directions and d = u_hat - v_hat, e = d/||d||.
    Since u_hat, v_hat and e are unit vectors, correlations against e are plain inner
    products, so
          corr(u_hat, e) - corr(v_hat, e) = <d, e> = <d, d>/||d|| = ||d||,
    which is the chordal distance. Conversely any statistic F that is 1-Lipschitz on the
    sphere obeys |F(u_hat) - F(v_hat)| <= ||u_hat - v_hat|| = ||d||. Hence the value is
    both attained and maximal.
    """
    uh, vh = normalise(u), normalise(v)
    d = [a - b for a, b in zip(uh, vh)]
    nd = norm(d)
    if nd == 0.0:
        raise ValueError("the hypotheses coincide as directions: no smooth test separates them")
    e = [x / nd for x in d]
    statistic: Callable[[Vector], float] = lambda x: dot(x, e) / (norm(x) * norm(e))
    sep = statistic(uh) - statistic(vh)
    return OptimalSmoothTest(
        direction=e,
        separation=sep,
        ceiling=nd,
        is_optimal=abs(sep - nd) <= 1e-12 * max(1.0, nd),
        statistic=statistic,
    )


def improvement_over(baseline_direction: Vector, u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    """Factor by which the optimal smooth test improves on correlating against a given
    baseline direction (typically the response w)."""
    uh, vh = normalise(u), normalise(v)
    b = normalise(baseline_direction)
    base = abs(dot(uh, b) - dot(vh, b))
    best = optimal_smooth_test(u, v).ceiling
    return float("inf") if base == 0.0 else best / base


if __name__ == "__main__":
    w = [1.0, 0.0]
    u = [math.cos(math.acos(0.558)), math.sin(math.acos(0.558))]
    v = [math.cos(math.acos(0.550)), math.sin(math.acos(0.550))]
    t = optimal_smooth_test(u, v)
    print(f"contrast direction     : ({t.direction[0]:+.6f}, {t.direction[1]:+.6f})")
    print(f"separation attained    : {t.separation:.10f}")
    print(f"smooth-class ceiling   : {t.ceiling:.10f}")
    print(f"optimal                : {t.is_optimal}")
    print(f"improvement over w     : x{improvement_over(w, u, v):.4f}")

algorithms.name: Cap-Capacity Audit for Graded Ladders of Hypotheses
algorithms.description: Research programmes frequently report a ladder of hypotheses, each rung claimed to be resolved from the previous one by a margin delta. Telescoping the per-rung gains gives a total of at least k*delta between the endpoints, while the power ceiling caps that same total at L*sqrt(2 eps) when the endpoints are aligned at 1 - eps; hence k <= L*sqrt(2 eps)/delta, independently of the dimension. This audit measures the endpoint alignment from the reported ladder (or accepts a stated one), computes the permitted number of rungs, and flags ladders whose claimed resolution exceeds what a statistic of the stated sensitivity can deliver. It also reports the chain bound obtained from the chordal triangle inequality, which is the companion estimate when per-link rather than endpoint alignments are known. Complexity is O(kn): one correlation per consecutive pair plus one for the endpoints. The audit is sound in one direction: failing it certifies over-reporting, whatever the sample size.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  f[0..k] : the reported ladder of hypothesis vectors (all nonzero)
       delta   : the per-rung gain the programme claims
       L       : the sensitivity of the statistic used
       eps     : optional endpoint alignment slack; measured if omitted
OUTPUT an audit record with a consistency verdict

 1  k   <- length(f) - 1
 2  rho <- corr(f[0], f[k]);  rho <- clamp(rho, -1, +1)
 3  if eps is absent then eps <- 1 - rho
 4  ceiling   <- L * sqrt(2 * eps)                  // power ceiling for the endpoints
 5  permitted <- floor(ceiling / delta)             // cap capacity
 6  claimed   <- k * delta                          // telescoped lower bound on the gain
 7  chain     <- sum over i<k of chord(f[i], f[i+1])// triangle-inequality companion bound
 8  consistent <- (claimed <= ceiling + tolerance)
 9  if not consistent then
10      REPORT: no statistic of sensitivity L supports k rungs of gain delta
11              inside a cap of alignment 1 - eps, at ANY sample size
12  RETURN (k, permitted, rho, chord(f[0],f[k]), ceiling, claimed, chain, consistent)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: cap-capacity audit for a graded ladder of hypotheses.

A research programme often reports not two hypotheses but a ladder of them, each rung
claimed to be resolved from the previous one by a margin delta. If the endpoints of the
ladder are aligned at 1 - eps, then telescoping the per-rung gains against the power
ceiling bounds the number of rungs by

        k  <=  L * sqrt(2 eps) / delta,

independently of the dimension. The audit below checks a reported ladder against that
bound, and also verifies the pairwise alignment claims that make it applicable.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = Sequence[float]


def dot(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))


def norm(u: Vector) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(dot(u, u))


def corr(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return dot(u, v) / (norm(u) * norm(v))


def chord(u: Vector, v: Vector) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(max(0.0, 2.0 - 2.0 * corr(u, v)))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LadderAudit:
    rungs_reported: int
    rungs_permitted: int
    endpoint_alignment: float
    endpoint_chord: float
    ceiling: float
    total_claimed_gain: float
    consistent: bool
    chain_bound: float          # k * sqrt(2 eps) from the triangle inequality


def capacity_bound(sensitivity: float, eps: float, delta: float) -> int:
    """Largest number of delta-separated rungs a stable statistic resolves in an eps-cap."""
    if delta <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("the per-rung margin must be positive")
    return int(math.floor(sensitivity * math.sqrt(2.0 * eps) / delta))


def audit_ladder(ladder: Sequence[Vector], delta: float, sensitivity: float = 1.0,
                 eps: float | None = None) -> LadderAudit:
    """Audit a reported ladder of hypothesis directions.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ladder      : the successive hypothesis vectors f_0, ..., f_k (all nonzero).
    delta       : the per-rung gain the programme claims its statistic achieves.
    sensitivity : the Lipschitz constant L of that statistic on the unit sphere.
    eps         : optional alignment slack for the endpoints; if omitted it is measured
                  from the ladder itself as 1 - corr(f_0, f_k).

    Complexity: O(k n) -- one correlation per consecutive pair plus one for the endpoints.

    The audit is *sound in one direction*: a ladder failing the bound cannot be supported
    by a statistic of the stated sensitivity, whatever the sample size.
    """
    if len(ladder) < 2:
        raise ValueError("a ladder needs at least two rungs")
    k = len(ladder) - 1
    rho = max(-1.0, min(1.0, corr(ladder[0], ladder[-1])))
    slack = (1.0 - rho) if eps is None else eps
    ceiling = sensitivity * math.sqrt(2.0 * slack)
    permitted = capacity_bound(sensitivity, slack, delta)
    per_step = [chord(ladder[i], ladder[i + 1]) for i in range(k)]
    return LadderAudit(
        rungs_reported=k,
        rungs_permitted=permitted,
        endpoint_alignment=rho,
        endpoint_chord=chord(ladder[0], ladder[-1]),
        ceiling=ceiling,
        total_claimed_gain=k * delta,
        consistent=(k * delta <= ceiling + 1e-12),
        chain_bound=sum(per_step),
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # The recorded instance: a two-rung ladder (floor, crossed) at margin 0.008.
    v = [math.cos(math.acos(0.550)), math.sin(math.acos(0.550))]
    u = [math.cos(math.acos(0.558)), math.sin(math.acos(0.558))]
    a = audit_ladder([v, u], delta=0.008, sensitivity=1.0, eps=1e-4)
    print(f"rungs reported   : {a.rungs_reported}")
    print(f"rungs permitted  : {a.rungs_permitted}")
    print(f"endpoint chord   : {a.endpoint_chord:.8f}")
    print(f"ceiling          : {a.ceiling:.8f}")
    print(f"claimed total    : {a.total_claimed_gain:.8f}")
    print(f"consistent       : {a.consistent}")

    # Two rungs at the same margin, claimed inside the same cap, are not supportable.
    x = [math.cos(math.acos(0.566)), math.sin(math.acos(0.566))]
    b = audit_ladder([v, u, x], delta=0.008, sensitivity=1.0, eps=1e-4)
    print()
    print(f"two-rung ladder consistent: {b.consistent} "
          f"(claimed {b.total_claimed_gain:.4f} vs ceiling {b.ceiling:.4f}); "
          f"measured endpoint chord {b.endpoint_chord:.5f} already exceeds the cap radius "
          f"{math.sqrt(2e-4):.5f}")

visualizations.name: The Correlation Cap and the Separation Profile of Every Smooth Test
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure. The left panel draws the unit circle with the response and the two hypothesis directions, plus a magnified inset showing the spherical cap of chordal radius sqrt(2 eps) with the two hypotheses inside it and the contrast direction joining them, making the sub-degree geometry visible. The right panel sweeps the test direction over the full circle and plots the separation achieved by correlating against it, overlaid with the chordal distance (attained exactly at the contrast direction), the Lipschitz ceiling sqrt(2 eps), and the recorded margin: the curve touches the chord and never rises above the ceiling.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: the correlation cap, drawn to scale, and the separation achievable
by correlating against each possible direction.

Left panel  : the unit circle with the two hypothesis directions and the spherical cap
              of chordal radius sqrt(2*eps), magnified in an inset so the 0.81-degree
              geometry is actually visible.
Right panel : the separation |corr(u_hat, e) - corr(v_hat, e)| as the test direction e
              sweeps the circle, together with the Lipschitz ceiling and the value
              attained by the contrast direction (u_hat - v_hat)/||u_hat - v_hat||.

Run:  python3 cap_geometry.py       (writes cap_geometry.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

READING_HI: float = 0.558
READING_LO: float = 0.550
EPS: float = 1.0e-4


def configuration() -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """u, v (the two hypothesis directions) and w (the response), all unit vectors in R^2."""
    w = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
    u = np.array([math.cos(math.acos(READING_HI)), math.sin(math.acos(READING_HI))])
    v = np.array([math.cos(math.acos(READING_LO)), math.sin(math.acos(READING_LO))])
    return u, v, w


def main() -> None:
    u, v, w = configuration()
    rho = float(u @ v)
    chord = float(np.linalg.norm(u - v))
    cap_r = math.sqrt(2 * EPS)

    fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.6))

    # ---------------- left: the circle and the cap ----------------
    th = np.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, 800)
    ax.plot(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), color="#30363d", lw=1)
    for vec, col, lab in ((w, "#8b949e", "response $w$"),
                          (u, "#3fb950", r"$\hat u$ (reads 0.558)"),
                          (v, "#f0883e", r"$\hat v$ (floor 0.550)")):
        ax.annotate("", xy=vec, xytext=(0, 0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col, lw=2))
        ax.text(vec[0] * 1.08, vec[1] * 1.08, lab, color=col, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-1.25, 1.35)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.25, 1.35)
    ax.set_title("Hypothesis directions on the unit circle", fontsize=11)
    ax.axis("off")

    # inset: magnify the cap
    ins = ax.inset_axes([0.58, 0.06, 0.40, 0.40])
    mid = (u + v) / np.linalg.norm(u + v)
    scale = cap_r * 1.6
    ins.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), cap_r, color="#58a6ff", alpha=0.18))
    ins.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), cap_r, color="#58a6ff", fill=False, lw=1.2))
    for vec, col in ((u, "#3fb950"), (v, "#f0883e")):
        d = vec - mid
        ins.plot([d[0]], [d[1]], "o", color=col, ms=7)
    du, dv = u - mid, v - mid
    ins.plot([dv[0], du[0]], [dv[1], du[1]], "--", color="#e6edf3", lw=1.4)
    ins.set_xlim(-scale, scale)
    ins.set_ylim(-scale, scale)
    ins.set_aspect("equal")
    ins.set_xticks([])
    ins.set_yticks([])
    ins.set_title(f"cap: radius {cap_r:.5f}\n(angular {math.degrees(math.acos(1-EPS)):.3f}$^\\circ$)",
                  fontsize=8)

    # ---------------- right: separation as a function of test direction ----------------
    angles = np.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, 2000)
    seps: List[float] = []
    for a in angles:
        e = np.array([math.cos(a), math.sin(a)])
        seps.append(abs(float(u @ e) - float(v @ e)))
    bx.plot(angles, seps, color="#58a6ff", lw=2, label="separation of a correlation test")
    bx.axhline(chord, color="#3fb950", ls="--", lw=1.6,
               label=f"chordal distance = {chord:.5f} (attained by the contrast direction)")
    bx.axhline(cap_r, color="#f85149", ls=":", lw=1.8,
               label=f"Lipschitz ceiling $\\sqrt{{2\\varepsilon}}$ = {cap_r:.5f}")
    bx.axhline(READING_HI - READING_LO, color="#f0883e", ls="-.", lw=1.4,
               label=f"recorded margin = {READING_HI - READING_LO:.3f}")
    contrast_angle = math.atan2(*(u - v)[::-1]) % (2 * math.pi)
    bx.plot([contrast_angle], [chord], "o", color="#3fb950", ms=8)
    bx.set_xlabel("angle of the test direction $e$ (radians)")
    bx.set_ylabel("separation $|\\,corr(\\hat u,e)-corr(\\hat v,e)\\,|$")
    bx.set_title(f"No smooth test beats the chord   (alignment $\\rho$ = {rho:.7f})", fontsize=11)
    bx.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
    bx.grid(alpha=0.2)

    fig.suptitle("The entire hypothesis test lives inside a cap of angular radius under $0.9^\\circ$",
                 fontsize=12)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("cap_geometry.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote cap_geometry.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The left panel plots, on log-log axes, the naive 1/sqrt(m) improvement one expects from replication against the actual ceiling for a stable statistic, which is exactly flat in m because correlation is replication-invariant; the recorded margin is marked for scale. visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: why replication cannot settle a near-threshold reading.

Left panel  : the naive expectation (resolution improving like 1/sqrt(N)) against the
              actual ceiling for a stable statistic, which is exactly flat in the number
              of replications because correlation is replication-invariant.
Right panel : the ceiling L*sqrt(2*eps) as a function of the alignment of the two
              hypotheses, with the recorded alignment window marked, and the sensitivity
              a statistic would need in order to return a decisive verdict.

Run:  python3 replication_ceiling.py      (writes replication_ceiling.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

EPS: float = 1.0e-4
MARGIN: float = 0.008


def main() -> None:
    cap_r = math.sqrt(2 * EPS)

    fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.2))

    # ---------------- left: replication ----------------
    ms = np.array([1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000])
    ceiling = np.full_like(ms, cap_r, dtype=float)
    naive = cap_r / np.sqrt(ms)
    ax.loglog(ms, ceiling, "o-", color="#f85149", lw=2.2,
              label="actual ceiling for any 1-Lipschitz statistic")
    ax.loglog(ms, naive, "s--", color="#8b949e", lw=1.6,
              label=r"naive expectation $\propto 1/\sqrt{m}$")
    ax.axhline(MARGIN, color="#f0883e", ls=":", lw=1.6,
               label=f"recorded margin {MARGIN}")
    ax.set_xlabel("number of replications $m$  (effective dimension $2m$)")
    ax.set_ylabel("largest separation a stable statistic can see")
    ax.set_title("Replication is invariant on the quantity that matters", fontsize=11)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    # ---------------- right: ceiling versus alignment ----------------
    rho = np.linspace(0.99, 0.9999999, 4000)
    chord = np.sqrt(2 - 2 * rho)
    bx.semilogy(rho, chord, color="#58a6ff", lw=2.2,
                label=r"ceiling at $L=1$:  $\sqrt{2-2\rho}$")
    bx.axhline(MARGIN, color="#f0883e", ls=":", lw=1.6, label=f"recorded margin {MARGIN}")
    lo, hi = 0.9999, 1 - MARGIN ** 2 / 2
    bx.axvspan(lo, hi, color="#3fb950", alpha=0.18,
               label=f"alignment window [{lo}, {hi:.6f}]")
    bx.axvline(lo, color="#3fb950", lw=1)
    bx.axvline(hi, color="#3fb950", lw=1)
    bx.set_xlabel(r"mutual alignment $\rho = corr(u,v)$ of the two hypotheses")
    bx.set_ylabel("ceiling (log scale)")
    bx.set_title("The ceiling collapses as the hypotheses align", fontsize=11)
    bx.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")
    bx.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower left")

    # annotate the required sensitivity at the recorded alignment
    bx.annotate(
        f"at $\\rho$ = 0.9999 the ceiling is {cap_r:.5f};\n"
        f"a decisive verdict needs sensitivity $L \\geq$ {1/cap_r:.2f}",
        xy=(0.9999, cap_r), xytext=(0.9925, 0.05),
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#e6edf3"), fontsize=9)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("replication_ceiling.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote replication_ceiling.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.description: An interactive laboratory for the central theorem. Four sliders control the alignment slack eps (logarithmically, from 1e-6 to 3e-2), the sensitivity L of the test statistic, the recorded margin delta between the two readings, and the number of replications m. A magnified rendering of the cap shows the two hypothesis directions, their chord, the contrast direction and the decision boundary of a threshold rule, while a live table reports the chordal and angular cap radii, the power ceiling, the sensitivity a decisive verdict would need, the alignment ceiling 1 - delta^2/2, the cap capacity in rungs, and the effective dimension after replication. A bar chart compares what each statistic can actually see: the response correlation, the optimal contrast correlation, the ceiling, and the discontinuous threshold rule. The panel also detects geometrically infeasible settings, where the requested margin cannot fit inside the requested cap, and states the reason. The intended discovery is visceral: dragging the replication slider changes the effective dimension by orders of magnitude and changes the ceiling by nothing at all.

Spherical-Cap Power Ceiling Explorer

Two competing hypotheses are realised by predictor directions on the unit sphere. If they correlate at 1 − ε, they sit inside a cap of chordal radius √(2ε) — and every statistic that changes by at most L per unit of movement on the sphere is forbidden from separating them by more than L·√(2ε). No sample size appears in that bound. Move the sliders and watch what the geometry permits.

interactive_demos.description: A hands-on demonstration of what escaping the ceiling actually costs. The predictor is dragged across the cap on a horizontal axis calibrated in correlation units, with the two hypotheses (the reading 0.558 and the floor 0.550) marked; a second slider sets the threshold cut and a third applies a perturbation to the predictor, expressed as a fraction of the cap radius. The canvas draws the smooth statistic as a gentle line whose total rise across the entire cap is the ceiling sqrt(2 eps) = 0.01414, and the threshold rule as a step of height 1 at the cut, with the current predictor and its perturbed copy both marked. A live panel reports both statistics before and after the perturbation and announces when the verdict flips. Users discover for themselves that the sharp test buys its decisiveness with an answer that can reverse under a perturbation far smaller than the cap itself.
interactive_demos.html:
Smooth vs. Discontinuous: the Brittleness Trade

The power ceiling says a stable statistic cannot separate two nearly-parallel hypotheses. A threshold rule can — completely. The catch is what happens when the predictor is nudged. Drag the predictor across the cap and watch the two statistics respond: the smooth one crawls, the sharp one snaps. The angular scale here is under one degree from end to end.

interactive_layout:
# A Ceiling You Cannot Buy Your Way Past ## 1. The stuck dial An experimental programme has pre-registered a threshold: the effect counts as present once a pooled correlation between predictor and response reaches $0.550$. The reading comes back as $0.558$ — over the line by eight thousandths — with a resampling interval that straddles the floor. The recorded verdict is the honest one: *approaching, not crossed*. The reflex is to collect more data. Noise falls like $1/\sqrt{N}$; surely enough runs settle it. This page is about a geometric obstruction that makes that reflex fail — not because the effect is small or the noise large, but because **the two competing hypotheses are almost the same object**, and almost every statistic anyone computes is blind to differences that small, by an amount that does not depend on the sample size at all. By the end you will be able to state the ceiling, see why replication is powerless against it, find the single best test that respects it, and understand exactly what you must give up to escape it. --- ## 2. Hypotheses are points on a sphere Everything follows from one translation. The experiment reports $$\operatorname{corr}(u, w) \;=\; \frac{\langle u, w\rangle}{\|u\|\,\|w\|},$$ which is unchanged when the predictor $u$ is rescaled by a positive number. So the experiment never sees $u$; it sees only the **direction** $\hat u = u/\|u\|$, a point on the unit sphere. Two rival hypotheses — "the dial reads $0.558$" and "the dial sits exactly on the floor $0.550$" — become two points $\hat u, \hat v$ on that sphere. The empirical fact that starts the whole analysis is that those two points can be chosen **extremely close together**: there are realisations of the two readings against a common response with $$\operatorname{corr}(u, v) \;\ge\; 0.9999 .$$
How close is a correlation of 0.9999, really? (click to reveal the computation) For unit vectors, the correlation *is* the cosine of the angle between them. So $$\text{angle} \;=\; \arccos(0.9999) \;=\; 0.0141423\ldots \text{ radians} \;=\; 0.81027^\circ .$$ Less than nine-tenths of one degree. If you drew both hypotheses as arrows a metre long, their tips would be $1.4$ centimetres apart. Every possible version of "crossed" and every possible version of "not crossed" lives inside that patch.
--- ## 3. The chordal identity: the one line everything rests on Expand the squared distance between the two directions: $$\|\hat u - \hat v\|^2 \;=\; \|\hat u\|^2 - 2\langle \hat u,\hat v\rangle + \|\hat v\|^2 \;=\; 2 - 2\operatorname{corr}(u,v),$$ because unit vectors have length $1$ and their inner product is exactly the correlation. So $$\boxed{\;\|\hat u - \hat v\| \;=\; \sqrt{2 - 2\operatorname{corr}(u,v)}\;}$$ and if $\operatorname{corr}(u,v) \ge 1-\varepsilon$ then the two hypotheses are at most $\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$ apart. With $\varepsilon = 10^{-4}$ this is $\sqrt2/100 = 0.0141421\ldots$ That number — the **cap radius** — is going to govern everything that follows.
The angular version, for the geometrically minded The angle and the chord are related by $\sqrt{2-2c} = 2\sin(\theta/2)$ where $\theta = \arccos c$. [Jordan's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan%27s_inequality) $\sin x \ge 2x/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ then gives $$\arccos c \;\le\; \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{2-2c},$$ so the angular radius of the cap is never worse than $\pi/2$ times the chordal radius — and for near-unit correlations the two agree to five decimal places.
--- ## 4. The ceiling, and the sliders that make it obvious Call a statistic $F$ **stable**, or $L$-Lipschitz on the sphere, if nudging a unit-vector predictor by a distance $r$ changes the statistic by at most $Lr$. Every practical summary is stable: correlations, regression slopes, smoothed effect sizes, likelihood ratios of smooth models. Combining stability with the chordal identity gives the central result. > **Spherical-Cap Power Ceiling.** If $\operatorname{corr}(u,v) \ge 1-\varepsilon$ and $F$ is > $L$-Lipschitz on the sphere, then > $$|F(\hat u) - F(\hat v)| \;\le\; L\sqrt{2\varepsilon}.$$ Look at what is missing: the dimension $n$. **The sample size does not appear.** Play with it. Push the alignment slider toward $1$ and watch the ceiling collapse; push the sensitivity slider up and watch the price of a decisive verdict; push the replication slider as far as it goes and watch nothing happen at all. {{interactive_demo:0}}
Proof of the ceiling (two lines) $\hat u$ and $\hat v$ are unit vectors, so the sphere-Lipschitz hypothesis applies directly: $|F(\hat u)-F(\hat v)| \le L\|\hat u - \hat v\|$. The chordal identity turns $\operatorname{corr}(u,v)\ge1-\varepsilon$ into $\|\hat u - \hat v\| \le \sqrt{2\varepsilon}$. Multiply. $\blacksquare$ Reading it backwards is just as useful: a statistic achieving separation $\delta$ inside the cap must have $L \ge \delta/\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$. At $\varepsilon = 10^{-4}$, a *fully decisive* verdict ($\delta = 1$) demands $L \ge 100/\sqrt2 = 70.71$.
--- ## 5. Why replication is powerless Model $m$ repetitions of the experiment by repeating the coordinate vector $m$ times. Then every inner product is multiplied by $m$ and every norm by $\sqrt m$ — and in the *ratio* that defines the correlation, those cancel exactly: $$\operatorname{corr}(\operatorname{rep}_m u, \operatorname{rep}_m v) \;=\; \operatorname{corr}(u,v).$$ The correlation is replication-invariant, so the chord is, so the ceiling is. The $m$-fold replicated experiment lives in dimension $2m$ and obeys the *identical* bound $L\sqrt2/100$. {{visualization:1}} The left panel is the whole methodological story: the grey curve is what everyone expects from replication, the red line is what the geometry actually delivers. {{demo:1}} --- ## 6. Is the ceiling real? Sharpness and non-vacuity A bound nobody attains deserves suspicion. Two checks dispose of that worry. **Sharpness.** For any $L$, the *distance statistic* $F(x) = L\|x - \hat v\|$ is exactly $L$-Lipschitz (reverse triangle inequality) and satisfies $F(\hat v) = 0$, $F(\hat u) = L\|\hat u - \hat v\|$. The ceiling is met exactly. **Non-vacuity.** Correlation against a fixed unit response, $x\mapsto\operatorname{corr}(x,w)$, is exactly $1$-Lipschitz on the sphere by [Cauchy–Schwarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality): for unit $x,y,w$, $|\langle x,w\rangle - \langle y,w\rangle| = |\langle x-y,w\rangle| \le \|x-y\|$. So the experiment's own headline statistic sits inside the constrained class.
A subtlety worth pausing on: sphere-Lipschitz, not globally Lipschitz The map $x \mapsto \operatorname{corr}(x,w)$ is *not* Lipschitz on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$ — its slope blows up near the origin, where a tiny change in $x$ swings its direction wildly. Restricting the requirement to the unit sphere is exactly the right hypothesis: it is what the geometry uses, and it is what real statistics satisfy. Weakening a hypothesis while keeping the conclusion is usually where the real content of a theorem hides.
--- ## 7. The alignment window: the margin fights back The alignment $0.9999$ is achievable. But the recorded margin pushes in the *opposite* direction. Since correlation against the response is $1$-Lipschitz on the sphere, $$|\operatorname{corr}(u,w) - \operatorname{corr}(v,w)| \;\le\; \|\hat u - \hat v\| ,$$ so a reading gap of $\delta = 0.008$ forces the hypotheses at least $0.008$ apart, hence $$\operatorname{corr}(u,v) \;\le\; 1 - \frac{\delta^2}{2} \;=\; 0.999968 .$$ Combining, the alignment is pinned in a window of width $6.8\times10^{-5}$: $$0.9999 \;\le\; \operatorname{corr}(u,v) \;\le\; 0.999968 .$$ The recorded configuration is essentially the geometric extremum. There is nothing left to gain by hunting for a cleverer realisation of the two hypotheses. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 8. So what *is* the best test? If the ceiling is $0.0141$ and the recorded test achieves $0.008$, is there something better? Yes — and it is completely classical. Take the **contrast direction** $$e \;=\; \frac{\hat u - \hat v}{\|\hat u - \hat v\|}$$ and correlate against it. Then $$\operatorname{corr}(\hat u,e) - \operatorname{corr}(\hat v,e) \;=\; \langle \hat u - \hat v, e\rangle \;=\; \frac{\|\hat u - \hat v\|^2}{\|\hat u - \hat v\|} \;=\; \|\hat u - \hat v\| .$$ The separation is *exactly* the chord — which is exactly the ceiling. So the maximum over the whole stable class is attained, and attained by a correlation statistic. > **The smooth optimum is the chord.** No statistic that is $1$-Lipschitz on the sphere separates > $\hat u$ from $\hat v$ by more than $\|\hat u - \hat v\|$, and correlating against the contrast > direction achieves that value. {{visualization:0}} The right-hand panel sweeps every possible test direction and finds the maximum precisely at the contrast direction, precisely at the chord — never above it. {{algorithm:1}} And now the deflating arithmetic. The recorded response correlation separates the hypotheses by $0.008$; the optimal smooth test separates them by the chord, which the window pins between $0.008$ and $0.0141$. The prize for switching to the optimal smooth test is therefore at most $$\frac{\sqrt2/100}{0.008} \;=\; 1.7678 .$$ A factor of $1.77$ on a gap of $0.008$. **Optimising within the smooth class is not where the leverage is.** --- ## 9. How much can fit in the cap? Exactly one rung Programmes rarely test two hypotheses; they report ladders of them. Suppose a stable statistic gains at least $\delta$ at each rung of a ladder whose endpoints are aligned at $1-\varepsilon$. Telescoping gives a total gain of at least $k\delta$, while the ceiling caps the same total at $L\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$. Hence $$k \;\le\; \frac{L\sqrt{2\varepsilon}}{\delta} .$$ At the recorded numbers: $k \le 1.7678$, so $k \le 1$. And exactly one rung *is* resolvable — the response correlation gains the full $0.008$ between the two configurations. **The capacity of the cap is exactly one rung.** {{algorithm:2}}
What if the statistic is only Hölder continuous? Suppose $|F(x)-F(y)| \le C\|x-y\|^\alpha$ on the sphere for some exponent $0<\alpha\le1$. The same argument gives the ceiling $C(\sqrt{2\varepsilon})^\alpha$, and $\alpha=1$ recovers the Lipschitz case. At the recorded instance a full verdict requires $C \ge 70.71$ at $\alpha=1$, $C \ge 8.41$ at $\alpha = 1/2$, $C \ge 2.90$ at $\alpha = 1/4$. Lower exponents buy a milder constant only by making the statistic more singular at small scales — the modulus $r\mapsto Cr^\alpha$ has infinite slope at $0$ once $\alpha<1$. The obstruction never disappears; it only changes shape.
--- ## 10. The escape hatch — and its price Every impossibility theorem invites you to break its hypothesis. Here the hypothesis is continuity, and breaking it works spectacularly. Fix the cut $t = 0.554$, midway between the readings, and report $1$ if $\operatorname{corr}(x,w) \ge t$ and $0$ otherwise. On exactly the same configuration this rule separates the hypotheses by the maximum possible amount, $1$ — inside a cap of angular radius $0.81^\circ$. There is no contradiction: this rule is $L$-Lipschitz for **no** constant $L$. Given any candidate $L$, one can exhibit two unit vectors straddling the cut at distance smaller than $1/L$. Feel the trade for yourself: drag the predictor across the cap and perturb it. {{interactive_demo:1}}
The explicit failure of the Lipschitz property Take $w = (1,0)$, $s=\sqrt{1-t^2}$, $x = (t,s)$ — a unit vector with $\operatorname{corr}(x,w)=t$ exactly, so the rule outputs $1$. For small $d>0$ put $y = (t-d, s)$. A computation gives $t^2\|y\|^2 - (t-d)^2 = (1-t^2)\,d\,(2t-d) > 0$, so $\operatorname{corr}(y,w) = (t-d)/\|y\| < t$ and the rule outputs $0$. But $\|x-y\| = d$. Choosing $d < 1/(2(|L|+1))$ makes $L\|x-y\| < 1$, contradicting the Lipschitz inequality. $\blacksquare$
The dichotomy is unavoidable: | | Stable statistics | Threshold / rank statistics | |---|---|---| | Maximum separation here | $0.0141$ (at $L=1$) | $1$ | | Best member | correlation against the contrast direction | threshold at $t=0.554$ | | Effect of more data | none | none | | Local sensitivity | bounded | unbounded | | Under a $0.01^\circ$ nudge | changes by $\le 2\times10^{-4}$ | may flip entirely | Neither column is uniformly better. What the geometry forbids is having both. --- ## 11. Put it all together The full diagnostic run, end to end, on the recorded instance: {{demo:0}} --- ## 12. What to take away 1. **Alignment, not sample size, is the binding constraint.** Two hypotheses whose predictors correlate at $1-\varepsilon$ are separated by at most $L\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$ for any stable statistic, in any dimension. 2. **This is computable before any data are collected.** The alignment of two hypothesised predictors is a design-stage quantity. A pre-registration that couples a smooth statistic with two hypotheses aligned above $1-\delta^2/2$ is internally inconsistent — it has committed to a test that cannot deliver the margin it promises. 3. **The best smooth test is a projection onto the difference of the hypotheses**, and knowing that tells you exactly how little room is left inside the smooth class. 4. **Decisiveness costs continuity.** If you need a verdict, you must accept a statistic whose answer can flip under a perturbation smaller than a hundredth of a degree — and you should choose that knowingly. A near-threshold reading that refuses to settle after many replications is not always a weak effect. Sometimes it is two things less than a degree apart, being measured by an instrument that cannot resolve a degree. ### Where to read further - [Cauchy–Schwarz inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality) — the engine behind both the correlation bound and the $1$-Lipschitz property. - [Spherical cap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_cap) — the geometric object the whole hypothesis test lives inside. - [Lipschitz continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipschitz_continuity) and [Hölder condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6lder_condition) — the stability classes the ceiling applies to. - [Concentration of measure on the sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_of_measure) — the classical companion phenomenon, where Lipschitz functions on high-dimensional spheres are nearly constant for a different, probabilistic reason.
